definition: The discipline and technique of producing, conserving and maturing wine.
A trained wine professional specialised in wine service and wine-and-food pairing.
Root-destroying pest that killed nearly 90% of European vines in the late 1800s; vines now grow on American rootstocks.
The whole environment of the vine: climate, topography (height, slope, aspect) and soil.
Purplish-red pigment in red grape skins that colours red wine; falls after ripening.
Concentration of phenolic compounds in skin and seeds as grapes ripen.
Extracting colour (and tannin) from the skins; partial maceration gives rosé, none is needed for white.
Whole-grape fermentation behind the fruity, drink-now Vin Nouveau style (Beaujolais Nouveau).
Circulating the must over the skins during fermentation for fuller colour extraction.
Conversion of malic acid into softer lactic acid during maturation, by Pediococcus bacteria.
Noble rot: a fungus that dries grapes and concentrates their sugar, for dessert wines such as Sauternes.
Base wine with added alcohol, 15–22% alcohol and high sugar: Marsala, Sherry, Port, Madeira.
Blending about two-thirds of the barrel with the next year's wine to keep fortified wine consistent.
The blend of first-fermented base wines in the Méthode Champenoise.
Wine, sugar and yeast added to the bottled cuvée to start the second fermentation.
Tilting and turning bottles to gather the yeast in the neck.
Added after the frozen yeast plug is removed (à la volée), before the final cork.
Sparkling wine fermented in a stainless-steel (INOX) tank instead of the bottle.
Tasting with eyes, nose and tongue: visual, olfactory and taste-olfactory analysis.
The small silver tasting cup used in the past.
The 'tears' a wine leaves on the glass wall; close-set tears mean a consistent, high-alcohol wine.
The continuous stream of bubbles in a sparkling wine.
Smelling by direct inhalation.
Smelling via exhaled air, key in the taste-olfactory phase.
Varietal aromas that come with the grape, from terpenes in the skin.
Aromas from pressing, fermentation and early maturation, including the vinous note.
Aromas from long maturation via esterification with partial oxidation; vinous disappears.
Compounds abundant in grape skin that are the source of primary aromas.
Secondary aroma from complex alcohols; gone after long ageing.
Reaction that creates aromatic substances during maturation.
The wine label, in French / Italian.
Identification of a wine by production area together with winemaking technique and grape varietal.
The year of harvesting printed on the label.
A 'fantasy' brand name a producer adds beyond the designation.
Aged in cask or barrel longer than the designation requires.
At least 0.5% more alcohol than the designation's minimum.
The historic production zone of a long-established designation.
Sparkling wine with more than 85% of the cuvée from one good year.
Sparkling wine from Chardonnay only.
Sparkling wine from Pinot Noir only.
Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée: France's highest, strictest category (since 1930).
France's middle category, less regulated than AOC.
Best-terroir vineyards (~2%), labelled with the cru name and no village.
Second tier (~12%), labelled village + Premier cru.
Grenache–Syrah–Mourvèdre, the signature southern French blend.
Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita: Italy's highest designation, controlled and quality-guaranteed.
Denominazione di Origine Controllata: Italy's largest designation, usually medium quality.
Indicazione Geografica Tipica: quality wine made outside DOC/DOCG rules (many Super Tuscans).
Vino da Tavola: wine made to no specification.
Tuscan wine (often Bordeaux grapes) made outside DOC rules; first in the 1960s.
Aromatic sparkling wine from a single fermentation in sealed tanks, stopped early to keep sugar.
